title: Reading Might Be One of the Best Health Hacks
excerpt: Reading has become one of the simplest habits I've added to my routine. I'm aiming for one book every two weeks, and I'm finding that 30 minutes with a book feels very different from 30 minutes scrolling on my phone. There may even be some interesting long-term health benefits.
content:
I've started to think of reading as a bit of a life hack.

For a long time, reading was something I did occasionally. I'd read a book, then go weeks or months without picking another one up. There was nothing wrong with that, but it wasn't really a habit.

Recently I've been trying to read at least one book every two weeks. I won't always hit that target, and I'm not interested in racing through books just so I can say I've read more of them. The target is just a way of making reading part of my normal routine, and I've found I genuinely feel better for it.

Spending 30 minutes reading feels very different from spending 30 minutes scrolling through my phone. With a book, I'm concentrating on one thing: taking in ideas, following an argument or getting lost in a story. My brain gets to stay with something instead of jumping between notifications, videos, headlines and whatever the algorithm puts in front of me next. That on its own seems like a pretty good reason to read more.

## It might be good for your brain too

What's made the habit even more interesting to me is that some research suggests reading may have longer-term benefits as well.

One longitudinal study followed 1,962 adults aged 64 and over in Taiwan for up to 14 years. People who reported reading more frequently were less likely to experience cognitive decline during the follow-up period.

Another looked at 3,635 adults from the US Health and Retirement Study and found an association between book reading and lower mortality over 12 years. The researchers also found that cognition appeared to play a role in that relationship.

I wouldn't take either study to mean that reading will make you live longer or prevent cognitive decline. They're observational, so they can show an association but can't prove that reading caused the difference. People who read regularly may differ from non-readers in plenty of other ways.

I still find the findings interesting, though. If something as simple as reading a book might be good for your brain, gives you a break from your phone and helps you learn new things, it seems an easy habit to make room for.

## My two-week rule

That's why I like the idea of one book every two weeks. It gives me something concrete to aim for without turning reading into a competition.

Some books will take longer and some will be much quicker. There will be weeks when life gets in the way and I don't manage it, and I'm fine with that. I'm less bothered about finishing exactly 26 books a year than about building a habit where picking up a book becomes the obvious thing to do when I've got half an hour to spare.

I've noticed another benefit too: reading gives me a reason to put my phone down. I don't need another productivity system or a complicated routine to make that happen. I just need a book and a bit of time.

## A pretty good investment

The more I think about it, the more reading seems like one of those habits where the potential upside is much bigger than the effort.

It costs very little. You don't need a gym membership or any special equipment, you can do it almost anywhere, and you can choose whatever interests you. You can learn about something new, deepen your understanding of something you already care about, see the world from somebody else's perspective or just disappear into a good story for a while. And if the research is right, there may be some longer-term benefits thrown in.

I'm not going to pretend that reading 26 books a year will transform my life. But regularly putting something new into my head feels like a pretty good investment in myself, so I'll keep going with one book every two weeks.
